items.claim: The row's onset at 50:41 and its close at 50:43 are both well-grounded, and its two Hebrew-to-English citations are precisely scoped to the same span.
items.evidence: The opening splice (byte tier) matches the paired WEB clause, “Behold, a people comes from the north,” at the same extent, and the fresh third-person army description at 50:41 follows directly on the closure formula ending the preceding verse, supporting a scene-shift onset rather than continuous description. The closing splice at 50:43 (byte tier) likewise matches its paired WEB quote, “Anguish has taken hold of him, pains as of a woman in labor,” at the same extent. The disclosed parallel to the Damascus oracle at 49:24 is byte-accurate: both verses share the anguish-and-labor-pang collocation while differing in their onset verb, so the parallel is correctly scoped as shared idiom rather than overstated as verbatim recurrence. The rejected alternative correctly treats the lion-from-the-Jordan material opening at 50:44 as its own template, independently paralleling 49:19, rather than folding it forward into the army-approach description.

items.claim: The setumah cited to close the row at 50:46 is not disclosed as single-witness, unlike the parallel setumah citations at the neighboring verses in this span.
items.evidence: Jer.50.46 (MT) is marked SAMEKH in the parashah inventory, so the claim that a setumah closes the unit there is accurate on its own terms. Every other setumah citation at the neighboring verses in this span (the closing marks at 51:14, 51:19, and 51:24) is disclosed with an explicit single-witness qualifier, consistent with the owner-ruled parashah policy that single-witness disclosure is required on every citation of that layer. This row's own closing sentence, stating that a setumah closes the unit at 50:46, carries no single-witness qualifier anywhere in the row, an isolated gap against that pattern. The ketiv/qere claim at 50:44, a doubled object-suffix spelling corrected from an unpointed to a pointed plural form, is itself byte-accurate and confirmed in the inventory, so the defect is confined to the missing disclosure on the closing mark, not to the mark's existence or the ketiv/qere reading.

items.claim: The koh-amar-YHWH onset at 51:1 is correctly attributed to the narrator's own direct oracle rather than a quoted human mouth, and the row correctly treats the writer-part boundary at 50:46/51:1 as a row-internal seam within the continuing nations-oracle parent.
items.evidence: The byte text of 51:1 opens with the divine-formula collocation exactly as claimed, with no embedding letter, false prophet, or other quoted speaker in view at this onset, so the frame-ownership hazard that attaches to koh-amar elsewhere in the book, where the formula is placed in a false prophet's own mouth, does not bear here. The row discloses the setumah closing the immediately preceding verse (50:46) as single-witness and explicitly states the nations-oracle parent continues unbroken across the writer-part boundary there, correctly keeping a part seam from being read as a parent seam. The closing grounds clause at 51:5, introduced by the causal particle, is a reasonable characterization of the verse's own syntax, and the rejected alternative correctly anticipates the discourse-imperative onset that follows as the next tier-1 seam.

items.claim: The discourse-imperative onset at 51:6 is a sound tier-1 seam, and the row's granularity call folding the embedded foreign voice at 51:9 into the same unit is correctly reasoned rather than reflexively split.
items.evidence: The byte text of 51:6 opens with the plural flight-imperative exactly as claimed, marking a clear shift from the oracle's grounds clause closing the preceding unit to direct address urging escape. The ketiv/qere at 51:9, a doubled healing-verb spelling, is confirmed in the inventory, and the row's own reasoning that the embedded first-person foreign voice at that verse is quoted speech without its own koh-amar or word-event marker, and so does not independently trigger a cut, correctly applies the rule that rows cut only at tier-1 internal seams. The rejected alternative names this same embedded-voice split as a real rival and gives a specific, byte-grounded reason for setting it aside rather than an unsupported preference.

items.claim: The second discourse-imperative onset at 51:11 is a sound tier-1 seam distinct from the flight command opening the preceding unit, and the row correctly reads the closing setumah at 51:14 as corroboration rather than as its own boundary driver.
items.evidence: The byte text of 51:11 opens with the plural sharpen-the-arrows imperative exactly as claimed, mobilizing the Medes against Babylon in language distinct from the flight command and foreign lament preceding it, supporting a fresh discourse-imperative seam rather than continuous material under one decree. The ketiv/qere at 51:13, a dwelling-on-many-waters verb spelling, is confirmed in the inventory. The row's own reasoning that the closing self-oath formula at 51:14 is followed by no further koh-amar or word-event onset, so the setumah there functions as corroboration rather than a driver, correctly applies the closure-corroboration standard used elsewhere for dense recurring devices.

items.claim: All three original-language citations in the row pair a Hebrew splice with a curly-quoted WEB clause taken from elsewhere in the same verse rather than the clause the Hebrew actually covers, so gloss extent does not equal splice extent at any of the three, even though the row's underlying genre-shift and doxology-twin argument is independently sound.
items.evidence: At 51:15 the Hebrew splice (byte tier) covers the verse's opening clause, matching WEB's “He has made the earth by his power,” but the row instead pairs it with the curly-quoted “He has established the world by his wisdom,” the verse's second clause. At 51:16 the Hebrew splice covers only the verse's opening adverbial phrase, matching WEB's “When he utters his voice,” but the row pairs it with “there is a roar of waters in the heavens,” the main clause that follows. At 51:19 the Hebrew splice covers only the verse-final divine-name formula, matching WEB's “Yahweh of Armies is his name,” but the row pairs it with “The portion of Jacob is not like these,” the verse's opening clause. Each WEB phrase quoted is itself verbatim and accurately drawn from the staged text; the mispairing runs in both directions rather than one consistent offset. The underlying literary claims survive independently of this citation defect: the 51:15 byte text is identical to 10:12, confirming the doxology-twin cross-reference; the 51:16 phrase is confirmed in the header inventory as an excluded false OAN-header candidate rather than a lamed-initial header; and setumah marks confirmed in the single-witness inventory bracket the unit at both 51:14 and 51:19. The closing sentence also describes the material beyond the row's own span with the row-positional phrase 'the row that follows' rather than a verse-anchored reference, where a neighboring citation in this same span uses content-anchored phrasing instead ('the material that follows').

items.claim: The row's closing citation pairs the Hebrew splice for the verse-final closing formula with a curly-quoted WEB clause drawn from an earlier part of the same verse, though the row's addressee-shift boundary argument itself does not depend on this citation.
items.evidence: At 51:24 the Hebrew splice (byte tier) covers only the verse-final formula, matching WEB's “says Yahweh,” but the row instead pairs it with the curly-quoted “all their evil that they have done in Zion in your sight,” a middle clause of the same verse; both phrases are verbatim WEB wording, just not the same span as each other. The row's own reading of this closing formula as closure corroboration rather than a boundary driver is correctly applied regardless of the mispairing. The fresh addressee shift opening the row at 51:20 is independently sound: its Hebrew splice covers the verse's opening words, and the paired WEB quote, “You are my battle ax and weapons of war,” is verbatim, covering that same opening sentence at a fuller extent than the Hebrew splice alone, a minor extent difference but not a mispairing to a different clause.
